newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's bond repo market set for further growth.
newsitem.headline: Japan's bond repo market set for further growth.

text.p: Japan's bond repo market is set to continue its expansion next fiscal year as more financial institutions are expected to participate, bankers say.

Expectations that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) will use the bond repo or repurchase market in its money market operations in future and a planned shortening of the settlement period for Japanese government bonds (JGBs) are likely to boost trades, they said.
"For a number of reasons, the bond repo market is likely to continue expanding in the next fiscal year," said an official at Nomura Trust and Banking Co Ltd. The fiscal year starts on April 1.
A BOJ official said the central bank was studying the possibility of using bond repos for money market operations in future, though no specific dates had been set.
This would enable the BOJ to expand its methods of conducting money market operations and give it greater flexibility, bankers said.
Under the current "T plus seven" rolling settlement, JGB settlement takes place seven business days after a trade. From April 21, this will be shortened to "T plus three".
"With the introduction of 'T plus three', the JGB market will move closer to the global standard," said the Nomura Trust official.
With rolling settlement, the time lag between trade and settlement is shortened, resulting in a greater need for bond dealers to borrow cash JGBs in the repo market.
Launched in April 1996, the bond repo market is distinct from the unsecured bond borrowing/lending market in that it involves borrowing and lending bonds with cash collateral.

The balance of the bond repo market at the end of January was 11.5957 trillion yen, according to the Japan Securities Dealers Association (JSDA). This compares with a market estimate of less than two trillion yen at the end of April 1996.
Bankers say the balance is soon likely to exceed that of the unsecured bond borrowing/lending market, which stood at 12.0545 trillion yen at the end of January.
"The repo market could expand into a 40 to 50 trillion yen market sometime next fiscal year," said the Nomura Trust official.
Bankers say that if big bond holders such as investment trusts and public funds participate, that could greatly boost liquidity in the market.
Investment trusts are hesitant as the funds they manage are under a number of separate accounts, meaning heavy administrative costs if they enter the market, bankers said.

Japan's Postal Life Insurance Bureau (Kampo), which holds some seven trillion yen worth of JGBs, is considering asking trust banks to manage part of its JGB holdings under securities trust contracts in the future, a Kampo official said.
Currently, Kampo conducts unsecured bond lending directly, but is unable to increase the amount due to a shortage of personnel, the official said.

An increasing number of smaller institutions such as regional banks and agricultural financial institutions, which have been hesitant to enter the market due to high costs, are starting to participate indirectly through securities trust contracts, bankers said.
Under a securities trust contract, trust banks manage and lend bonds on behalf of their clients.
The balance of Japanese trust banks' securities trust contracts stood at around 5.9 trillion yen at the end of September 1996.

"It is not easy for smaller financial institutions to participate directly in the repo market due to high systems costs and a lack of skilled personnel. Also, bond repo is not necessarily a highly profitable business," said Naoshi Hayase, general manager of the corporate finance and trust department at IBJ Trust and Banking Co. Ltd.
"For those reasons, these institutions are choosing to participate indirectly through securities trusts," Hayase said.
His bank manages some 900 billion yen worth of bonds in the repo market under securities trust agreements.
